strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile problem: predicting human response times when environmental cues evolve during a decision. Combining task-trained representations, a behavioral baseline, and sequential modulation is a plausible and useful modeling direction.

The two-day study provides 21,157 responses from 36 retained participants across four feedback regimes. Evaluating individual, group, pooled, and leave-one-participant-out models offers useful perspectives on personalization and generalization.

The hybrid model consistently improves aggregate MAPE over the supplied Pure DRL baseline across the four evaluation settings. For example, leave-one-participant-out MAPE decreases from 0.3037 to 0.2905. The feature comparison also supports the usefulness of the task-trained representation.
The framework diagram and component descriptions make the overall approach understandable, and the manuscript provides links to data, models, and implementation code.
weaknesses: The central cognitive interpretation is insufficiently supported. Methods describe the DDM component as a sigmoid trajectory terminating at an SVC probability, without specifying a diffusion process or justifying this probability-to-boundary mapping. Training rewards depend only on final response-time error, so different intermediate trajectories can explain the same observation. Consequently, Fig. 7 does not establish that the learned actions recover human evidence accumulation or stress mechanisms. Nonzero 'time pressure effects' in the no-pressure group further suggest that the actions also compensate for baseline prediction errors.

The main comparison does not isolate the proposed accumulation mechanism. Pure DRL uses full-video Inception features, different action scaling, and a different episode structure, while the hybrid model processes individual frames. These differences confound both prediction and training-time comparisons. Matched ablations, a supervised predictor with pressure information, and a conventional DDM with stimulus-dependent parameters would better establish the contribution relative to existing approaches. Removing or shuffling frame information would also test whether fine-grained visual dynamics provide useful information.

The training protocol for the SVM stages is unclear. Although these models purportedly estimate performance without pressure, the manuscript does not identify precisely which observations train them or whether they are refitted exclusively within every training split, especially leave-one-participant-out evaluation. This prevents verification of both leakage prevention and the interpretation of subsequent corrections as pressure effects.

The reported prediction gains lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-seed results; some are small, such as pooled MAPE of 0.2999 versus 0.3034. Participant-level paired analyses would help establish their reliability. Moreover, all evaluations use one arithmetic task and the same repeating progress-bar stimulus, limiting evidence for the broader claims about dynamic environmental stress and transfer to other stimuli.

Important reproduction details are missing, including the exact sigmoid construction, the modulation factor lambda, numerical thresholds for the adaptive feedback rule, and operational criteria for excluding extreme participants and handling response times beyond ten seconds. Smaller reporting issues also warrant correction: Results describes 50 participants although 36 enter the final analysis, and the stated use of paired between-group post hoc tests needs clarification because the groups contain different participants.
